The first year, I grated potatoes, chopped onions, and watched. The uncle, made rich by a song, stacked three and dug in, talking critics and Koch—everyone crunching now, slathering applesauce, slurping tea—talking Rabin and Mehitabel, radio and Durrell, how a song is a poem or it isn’t a song, and vice versa. Finished, he pointed a greasy finger at me and said, “You can’t be a goy. You—I say it for all to hear—are an honorary Jew!” An impossible dream my latkes lived up to for five more years.

outputs.L2:
In year one, I shredded the potatoes, diced the onions, and observed. By year two, I was loading every ingredient except the eggs into the machine, announcing that I would make the latkes—and then making them. My wife, still a mystery to me, carried my mound of golden, crunchy wonders to the gathering. In that apartment—though my in-laws called it a house—books had been put away, joking had ceased, and money held no value. New-wave music pounded from one side while marijuana smoke drifted from the other. There, she had once dropped to her knees and told the nobody still paying attention, “No more, no, no more, no,” shaping the indispensable prayer with the lips of a three-year-old.

An uncle who had grown wealthy from a single song took three latkes from the stack and began eating. As everyone crunched, spooned on applesauce, and noisily drank tea, he spoke of reviewers and Koch, of Rabin and Mehitabel, of radio and Durrell, and of how a song either qualifies as a poem or fails as a song—and the reverse as well. When he finished, he aimed an oil-slicked finger at me and declared, “You cannot be a goy. You—let me proclaim this before everyone—are a Jew by honorary appointment!”

For another five years, against all likelihood, my latkes proved worthy of that fantasy. Afterward came the cries. Afterward, the dust.

In the first year, the speaker learned how to make latkes by helping with the simplest tasks: grating potatoes, chopping onions, and carefully observing the more experienced cooks. By the second year, he had gained enough confidence to prepare the latkes himself for a lively family gathering.

During the feast, everyone ate generously, drank tea, and joined in animated conversation. Their discussion moved easily from politics and literature to radio, songs, and the connection between poetry and music. The latkes were warmly received, and one uncle offered especially memorable praise, declaring the speaker an “honorary Jew.”

This latke-making tradition continued for another five years, becoming a meaningful part of the family’s shared celebrations. Eventually, however, the custom came to an end, overshadowed by grief and loss.
outputs.L4:
The first year, I stood at the edge of the kitchen and watched. The room was crowded with relatives talking over one another, correcting one another, laughing, arguing about politics, history, and the proper way to grate a potato. Oil snapped in the frying pan. Someone sang a few lines of an old song; someone else complained that the tune was wrong. I understood almost none of the Hebrew or Yiddish that flashed through the conversation, but I understood the warmth of the room and the invitation contained in being allowed to remain there.

The second year, they gave me a peeler. I worked slowly while the others moved with the assurance of people repeating gestures they had known all their lives. I was told not to take off too much of the potato, not to leave too much skin, not to let the peeled ones turn brown. Every instruction produced three conflicting instructions from another part of the kitchen. The family’s traditions seemed to live not in agreement but in the affectionate dispute over how things ought to be done.

By the third year, I was grating potatoes and onions. My eyes watered, my knuckles ached, and everyone made jokes at my expense. I learned to squeeze the mixture dry, though one aunt said I squeezed too hard and another said not hard enough. I learned that recipes could be arguments about memory: whose mother used flour, whose grandmother preferred matzo meal, who added an extra egg, who insisted that no true latke should be made in quite the way everyone else was making them.

The fourth year, I stood at the stove. That was the place of danger and judgment. I dropped spoonfuls of batter into the hot oil and tried to shape them before the edges set. Some fell apart. Some burned. Some were pale and heavy in the middle. But gradually I learned to listen for the right sound and to recognize the instant when the underside had crisped enough to turn. I lifted each latke carefully, let the oil drain, and laid it on paper while hands reached past me almost as quickly as I could cook.

By the fifth year, no one needed to tell me what to do. I arrived, rolled up my sleeves, and took my place in the kitchen. I grated, mixed, seasoned, and fried while conversation surged around me. The smells no longer seemed foreign. The noise no longer made me feel like a guest. When the first platter was carried into the dining room, the uncle who had watched my apprenticeship took a latke, bit through its crisp edge, and considered it with exaggerated seriousness.

Then he nodded.

“You,” he announced, “are now an honorary Jew.”

Everyone laughed, but beneath the laughter I heard something solemn. The words admitted me into a circle I had approached slowly, year by year. I knew that belonging could not truly be granted by a single taste or sentence, yet I carried his declaration as if it were a blessing. For five years it remained with me: the crowded kitchen, the bright oil, the overlapping voices, and the certainty that I had been welcomed.

Then came the wailing.

Then came the dust.

In a single terrible morning, the familiar world disappeared behind smoke and ash. Voices that had once filled rooms with argument and laughter broke into cries, frantic questions, names repeated into telephones and into the air. Dust settled over streets, clothing, photographs, and memory. It covered the city’s ordinary distinctions and left everything gray.

The uncle’s words still lived in me, but now they belonged to a vanished before. What had felt permanent—the kitchen, the family, my place among them—became fragile. Yet even after the wailing, even beneath the dust, I remembered his nod and the latke in his hand. I remembered being told that I belonged.
outputs.L5:
### Koch and Rabin: Leadership in Public Life

Ed Koch and Yitzhak Rabin were influential political leaders who served their communities in very different contexts. Koch, the outspoken mayor of New York City from 1978 to 1989, became known for his energetic personality, direct communication style, and efforts to restore the city’s financial stability.

Rabin, meanwhile, was an Israeli military commander and statesman who served twice as prime minister of Israel. He played a central role in the Oslo peace process and shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with Shimon Peres and Yasser Arafat. His assassination in 1995 made him an enduring symbol of the risks and hopes associated with pursuing peace.

Although Koch and Rabin followed different paths, both demonstrated how individual leadership can shape public debate and leave a lasting political legacy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical prose poem about a non-Jewish man learning to make latkes for his wife’s family, earning the title “honorary Jew,” and ending years later with sudden tragedy.
counterfactuals.output:
The first winter he stood in her mother’s kitchen, sleeves rolled above his pale, freckled arms, holding an onion as if it were a difficult question.

“Grate,” her mother told him, pointing to the box grater. “And don’t be brave about the tears.”

He was not Jewish. He knew this the way he knew he had married into a house full of inherited songs: carefully, gratefully, from the doorway at first. He knew which drawer held the candles, but not the blessings; knew that every recipe began with *a little* and ended with *you’ll know*; knew history sat at the table even when no chair had been set for it.

He grated potatoes until his knuckles reddened, wrung them in a dish towel, watched starch gather like snowmelt at the bottom of the bowl. Egg, onion, salt. Her father advised more pepper. An aunt contradicted him. Three cousins leaned over the oil, each claiming the flame was too high or too low. His wife laughed from the table, chin in her hand, as if she had always known he would find his way into this argument.

The first latke came apart.

The second burned at the edges.

The third emerged crisp and ragged, gold as a small, domestic sun.

Her grandmother tasted it without expression. Everyone waited. Oil snapped in the silence.

Finally she nodded.

“Honorary Jew,” she declared.

The room erupted. Someone filled his glass. Someone kissed his cheek. His wife slipped her oily fingers through his, and for the rest of the night he stood at the stove, turning potatoes into light.

Years accumulated around that skillet. Children arrived and grew tall enough to grate, then old enough to complain. The grandmother’s chair became empty. Her father forgot where the candles were kept. New voices learned the old blessings, stumbling over syllables while he tended the pan. He developed rules: squeeze the potatoes twice, never crowd the oil, sacrifice the first latke to the cook. Each December the title was renewed with ceremony and teasing, though by then no one remembered a holiday without him.

Then, one ordinary March morning, before coffee, before goodbye had understood it was goodbye, his heart stopped.

There was no candle ready for such darkness. No recipe. No argument loud enough to call him back.

When winter came, his wife found the skillet beneath the stove. She set it on the burner and stood for a long time with one hand on its handle. Around her, the family gathered—older, diminished, still arriving. They grated onions. They did not pretend the tears belonged only to onions.

The first latke came apart.

The second burned at the edges.

The third emerged crisp and ragged, gold as the small sun he had carried for them all those years.

No one spoke. They passed it from hand to hand, each taking a piece.

And in the sudden quiet after the blessing, the oil kept shining.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph memoir vignette about Hanukkah, marriage, eccentric intellectual in-laws, food, cultural belonging, and the shadow of 9/11. Use compressed, poetic language.
counterfactuals.output: That first Hanukkah of our marriage, under the long ash-shadow of 9/11, I stood in my in-laws’ kitchen grating potatoes while my father-in-law—an exiled classicist in a moth-eaten cardigan—argued that the Maccabees had ruined everything, and my mother-in-law, who annotated cookbooks in three languages, salted the latkes without looking up from Spinoza. My husband lit the menorah in the window, each flame trembling against a city still flinching at sirens, and I carried in bowls of applesauce and sour cream like small passports. Oil snapped; onions sweetened; somebody disputed translation, somebody sang off-key. I knew only half the blessings and none of the family footnotes, yet when they nudged me closer to the candles, making room with their elbows and their ferocious opinions, belonging arrived not as revelation but appetite: smoke in my hair, grease on my fingers, his hand finding mine beneath the table.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental first-person piece in which latke-making becomes a ritual of acceptance into a Jewish family. Include lively dinner-table conversation, an uncle connected to songwriting, and the refrain-like ending: “Then the wailing. Then the dust.”
counterfactuals.output:
The first test was the onion.

“Don’t cry into the bowl,” Aunt Mira said. “It makes the latkes sentimental.”

“I thought sentiment was the main ingredient,” I said.

“No,” said Grandma Ruth from the table. “That’s guilt.”

Everyone laughed except me, because I was holding half an onion in one hand and the family grater in the other, and it had occurred to me that this might not be a joke.

The grater was older than the state of Israel, younger than the oldest argument in the room, and bent slightly in the middle. Its handle had once been red. Generations of knuckles had polished it down to something like bone.

I grated.

My eyes flooded.

“Good,” Grandma said. “Now you look related.”

—

They had invited me for dinner many times before, but this night was different. This night, Mira tied her blue apron around my waist. This night, Ruth surrendered the potatoes. This night, my partner, Leah, was told to sit down and stay out of it.

“She has no patience,” Ruth explained.

“I have patience,” Leah protested.

“You buy shredded potatoes in a bag.”

“That’s efficiency.”

“That’s exile.”

Uncle Daniel lifted his wineglass. “I’m putting that in a song.”

“You put everything in a song,” Mira said.

Daniel had written jingles in the eighties, folk songs in the nineties, and one chorus everyone swore had been stolen by a famous musician, though the identity of the thief changed depending on how much wine had been poured. He tapped rhythms on tabletops, hummed into his soup, rhymed *menorah* with *Fedora* and, once, disastrously, *flora*.

Now he watched me squeeze water from the grated potatoes.

“Tighter,” he said. “You’ve got to wring out the sorrow.”

“Don’t listen to him,” Leah said. “His last album was called *Wring Out the Sorrow*.”

“EP,” Daniel corrected.

“Three songs.”

“Three and a reprise.”

—

The second test was oil.

Oil remembers heat. Oil is a small shining history. Oil waits in the pan like a held breath.

“How do I know when it’s ready?” I asked.

Mira flicked in a shred of potato. It hissed instantly.

“When it answers back.”

At the table, everyone was answering back.

“Applesauce,” said Leah’s father.

“Sour cream,” said Mira.

“Both,” said Daniel.

“Both is cowardice,” said Ruth.

“Both is diplomacy,” I called from the stove.

There was a pause.

Then Ruth nodded once.

The family grater had taken a crescent from my thumb. Onion had entered my eyes, my hair, the wool of my sweater. My hands smelled of earth and salt. The first latke broke apart when I flipped it.

No one spoke.

The second burned.

Daniel began humming a funeral march.

“Stop that,” Mira said, hitting him with a dish towel.

The third held.

It came up from the oil ragged at the edges, gold shading toward brown, no perfect circle but a continent, a weather map, a little sun with crisp rays. I set it on the paper bag they used for draining.

Ruth rose from her chair.

She crossed the kitchen slowly, leaning on the counter but refusing the arm Leah offered. She tore off a corner, blew on it, tasted.

The whole room waited.

“Needs salt,” she said.

Everyone exhaled.

Then she ate the rest.

—

We fried in batches.

This is how ritual works: repetition until fear becomes rhythm.

Scoop. Press. Slide.

Hiss.

Wait.

Turn.

At some point I stopped asking when. My wrist learned. The spoon learned. The oil taught me its alphabet: whisper, crackle, warning, applause.

Behind me, dinner gathered volume.

“Daniel,” Leah’s father said, “tell her about the song you wrote for your bar mitzvah.”

“I did not write it for my bar mitzvah.”

“You rhymed *Torah* with *more-ah*.”

“I was thirteen.”

“You sang seven verses.”

“I had a lot to say.”

“You still do,” Ruth said.

Daniel pointed at her. “That’s where the gift comes from.”

“The gift comes from your mother’s side,” Ruth replied. “From my side comes timing.”

I carried in the platter.

It was too heavy, too hot, too full. Hands reached toward it before I had set it down.

“Wait,” Mira cried. “Candles first.”

“Blessing first.”

“Picture first.”

“If you take a picture, they’ll get cold.”

“They’re already getting cold.”

“Daniel, stop eating.”

“I’m checking for poison.”

“You’ve checked four.”

“Thoroughness is love.”

And there it was: the family grammar. Every command meant *stay*. Every criticism meant *we have noticed you*. Every interruption meant *you are not alone here, even in your own sentence*.

Leah found my hand under the table. My thumb wore its small white bandage like a veil.

Ruth passed me the applesauce.

Not to Leah. Not to Mira.

To me.

“Next year,” she said, “use more onion.”

“Next year?”

“Don’t make me repeat myself.”

Across the table, Daniel struck a chord on an invisible guitar.

“Title,” he announced. “‘Use More Onion.’”

“No,” everyone said.

He sang anyway.

—

Later, after the candles collapsed into blue pools, after the platter showed only translucent commas of oil, after Daniel’s seventh verse and Ruth’s third complaint about it, Mira placed the old grater in my hands.

“Wash it,” she said.

It was not a gift. It was better. A gift can be admired and put away. This was a task, and after the task another task, an endless bright chain of them: grate, fry, feed, argue, return.

At the sink, potato starch clouded the water. Behind me, the family rose and collided—chairs scraping, plates stacking, three people insisting they would make coffee and no one making coffee. Leah leaned against my shoulder.

“Did I pass?” I whispered.

From the table, without turning, Ruth said, “Salt.”

I laughed. I salted the last latke. I ate it standing at the sink, over the wreckage of dinner, while Daniel tried to find a rhyme for *belonging* and everyone told him he was pronouncing it wrong.

Outside, snow began erasing the parked cars, the steps, the whole hard street.

Inside, they argued about who would take me home.

Then the wailing. Then the dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem about memory and loss that begins with the narrator watching others grate potatoes, follows his gradual mastery of latkes, and culminates in an uncle publicly declaring him an honorary Jew.
counterfactuals.output:
I began by watching others grate potatoes, their knuckles hovering above the silver teeth, their hands fluent in a language of caution and hunger. The kitchen windows clouded while onions surrendered their sharpness to the bowl. I was given small tasks: wring the shreds in a towel, gather stray skins, listen when the oil began its rain. The dead moved quietly among us then—my grandmother in the tilt of a wrist, my father in the salt pinched without measuring, the missing places at the table shining brighter than the plates.

Year by year, I learned. First the rough moons fell apart in the pan; then they held. I learned that too much flour smothers memory, that oil must be hot enough to welcome but not to punish, that patience has a sound: the steady hiss beneath conversation. Soon my latkes emerged crisp at the edges, tender at the center, each one a little browned archive. We ate them with applesauce, with sour cream, with stories revised by every mouth. Loss sat beside us and took what it always takes, but for an evening we made it eat too.

At the winter gathering, I carried in a platter stacked like gold coins rescued from a ruined kingdom. Everyone reached at once. My uncle bit into one, closed his eyes, and struck the table with his palm. Then he stood, lifted the latke as if it were evidence, and announced to the whole room, “From this day forward, he is an honorary Jew.” Laughter rose, glasses rang, and I bowed beneath the blessing and the joke. In the bright kitchen, among those who remained and those we could not stop remembering, the empty chairs seemed, for one fragrant moment, almost warm.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a dense, punctuation-driven literary monologue about a chaotic family feast in a New York apartment, blending humor, intellectual banter, Jewish identity, domestic tension, and a devastating final historical rupture.
counterfactuals.output:
By seven the apartment had become a republic of elbows: Uncle Lenny filibustering from the radiator (“Spinoza, fine, but would you let him manage a delicatessen?”), Aunt Ruth sawing the brisket into theological objections, my mother shouting from the kitchen that nobody appreciated heat as a concept—heat, not cooking, heat!—while the windows sweated onto West End Avenue and three taxis below conducted, by horn, a Talmudic dispute concerning a double-parked Buick; meanwhile the children tunneled under the table, the dog ate half a napkin and achieved innocence, and my father, who had been dead six years but remained chairman of every meal, was quoted against us: Your father liked the carrots thinner; your father never drank before soup; your father, God rest him, knew how to sit.

Sit! We were twenty-one people in four hundred square feet, balanced on folding chairs, piano benches, telephone books, and ancestral grievance. Cousin Miriam had brought a Columbia professor who said “diaspora” as though he had invented distance; Cousin Sol, who sold plumbing fixtures in Queens, asked whether diaspora came in chrome. The professor laughed incorrectly. This was noticed.

“Identity,” Miriam began.

“Eat,” said my mother.

“I’m saying identity is constructed.”

“So construct yourself a plate.”

“It’s not that simple.”

“Nothing with gravy is simple.”

Then came the annual inquiry: who was still Jewish, who was merely anxious, who had married out, who had married worse, who believed in God, who blamed Him personally, who fasted on Yom Kippur except for coffee, toast, and an egg; and because no family can discuss eternity without discussing real estate, Aunt Ruth asked what we paid for the apartment, Uncle Lenny lied on our behalf, my mother corrected him upward, and the professor—God preserve the educated—called rent control “a fascinating moral contradiction,” at which Sol told him to fascinate himself into the kitchen and bring more seltzer.

The feast advanced by catastrophe: soup spilled, crystal cracked, the kugel listed starboard; somebody accused somebody of voting Republican in 1972, somebody else cried because the napkins were not Grandma’s napkins, though no one could establish whose napkins they were. Outside, Manhattan glittered with its usual vulgar promise—sirens, neon, steam rising from the grates like the city’s own exhausted soul—and inside we passed the bread clockwise, the salt counterclockwise, blame in every direction.

Then my mother brought out the silver candlesticks.

Not lit—never lit; wrapped in a dish towel, blackened at the stems, one bent slightly inward as though listening.

“Those aren’t yours,” Aunt Ruth said.

My mother stood very still.

“No,” she said. “They were my sister’s.”

The room, which had survived philosophy, politics, indigestion, and love, stopped.

We knew there had been a sister; or we knew the outline of one, a grammatical absence, a pronoun no one conjugated. My mother placed the candlesticks between the brisket and the wine.

“She set the table the night before they came,” she said. “Łódź. September. She was twelve. She wanted everything ready for Shabbos.”

A taxi horn cried below; the radiator knocked; under the table a child whispered that the dog had found the bone.

“And then?” Miriam asked—softly now, without theory.

My mother looked at us: the crowded apartment, the stained cloth, the ridiculous abundance; twenty-one mouths arrested between hunger and history.

“There was no then,” she said.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
